title: Which step size wins?
hook: A ball hops down a valley. Which step size ends nearest the bottom?

knows: reading a curve on a graph
that a steeper slope means a bigger change

misconception: A bigger step size always gets gradient descent to the minimum faster.
objective: The learner can explain that each step moves (step size × slope), so a step size that is too small crawls, one that is too big overshoots and zigzags, and one past a limit flies away; the fastest is in the middle.

claims.text: Gradient descent moves each step downhill by the step size times the slope: x ← x − η·f′(x).
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016), §4.3 (gradient-based optimization).

claims.text: On the valley f(x) = x², the slope is 2x, so one step multiplies the position by (1 − 2η).
Starting at x = 4, ten steps with step size 0.05 or 0.95 both end about 1.39 from the bottom (one crawling, one zigzagging); with 0.45 the ball ends less than 0.001 from the bottom.
claims.source: Distance after n steps is |1 − 2η|^n · 4: 0.9^10 · 4 = 1.3947 for η = 0.05 and η = 0.95 (the stage shows 1.39); 0.1^10 · 4 = 4e-10 for η = 0.45. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): node (own loop x <- x - 2 eta x from 4): eta 0.05 -> 1.39471, eta 0.95 -> 1.39471 (fmtDist '1.39' both), eta 0.45 -> 4.0e-10 (fmtDist '< 0.001'). Stage run list and reveal match.

claims.text: On f(x) = x², any step size above 1 makes each step land farther from the bottom: at 1.05, ten steps from x = 4 end about 10.4 away.

Training real neural networks faces the same trade-off: too small a learning rate makes training slow, too large makes it oscillate or diverge, so the learning rate is often the most important setting to tune.
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016), §8.3.1 and §11.4.1 (learning rate as the most important hyperparameter); Bengio (2012), Practical recommendations for gradient-based training of deep architectures. v2: the verbatim quote was dropped because nobody had read it against the book (fact-check fix 3).

claims.text: Neural networks are trained with variants of gradient descent that update all of their parameters at once, and those can number in the millions.
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016), §6.5 and §8.3 (stochastic gradient descent); network sizes in §1.2.3.

claims.text: At step size exactly 1, the ball bounces between the same two spots forever (4 and −4, starting from 4).
claims.source: 1 − 2η = −1 at η = 1, so x → −x each hop; seen on stage as 'Bouncing between the same two spots forever.' Added by fact-checker from the stage messages; needs independent check.

claims.text: On this valley the ball gets to the bottom fastest where 1 − 2 × step size is zero: a step size of 0.5, which lands on the bottom in one hop (the stage has a 0.50 run).
claims.source: Distance after n hops is |1 − 2η|^n · 4, smallest when 1 − 2η = 0, i.e. η = 0.5. v2 reveal: 'Fastest is where it is zero: a step size of 0.5.' Needs independent check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): Derivation: distance after n hops = |1 - 2 eta|^n x 4, zero for n >= 1 iff eta = 0.5. node: eta 0.5 gives exactly 0 after one hop; over the slider grid 0.05..1.05 the best 10-hop distance is at 0.50. Stage message 'Landed on the bottom in one hop.' and a 0.50 preset exist.

claims.text: The stage's running message describes the hop just taken, not a future: 'Heading down; each hop is shorter than the last' for step sizes between 0.2 and 0.5 until the ball is within 0.05 of the bottom, then 'Now within 0.05 of the bottom.'
claims.source: v2 Demo.tsx message(): factor 1 − 2η in (0, 0.6] gives hops that shrink by that factor each time (4 × 0.6^n at η = 0.2: 2.40, 1.44, 0.86 ...), so each hop is shorter than the last; the 'within 0.05' branch tests the displayed distance. Replaces the v1 'Close to the bottom in a few hops' message that was false at hop 1 (fact-check fix 1). Needs independent check.

claims.text: On this valley the slope under the ball is 2 × its position, so the next hop is step size × slope (from the start at 4 with step size 0.05: 0.05 × 8 = 0.40); each hop multiplies the distance by 1 − 2 × step size, shown on the stage and giving 0.9 at step size 0.05, 0.1 at 0.45, 0 at 0.50 and −0.9 at 0.95.
claims.source: f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x; hop length η·|2x|; 1 − 2(0.05) = 0.9, 1 − 2(0.95) = −0.9, 1 − 2(0.45) = 0.1. Added v2 for the stage line 'Next hop = step × slope = …' and the reveal's three factors. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x. node: first hop at 0.05 = 0.05 x 8 = 0.40; factors 0.9, 0.1 (0.09999999999999998, shown 0.10), 0, -0.9 (shown '−0.90'). Stage line 'Next hop = 0.05 × slope 8.00 = 0.40. Distance × 0.90 per hop.' matches.

claims.text: For step sizes below 0.2 the running message says 'Slow: each hop covers under 40% of the distance left.'
claims.source: Stage message() branch factor > 0.6 (step size below 0.2). Hops at 0.05 are 0.40 of a 4.00 distance (10%), but at 0.15 the first hop is 1.20 (30% of the distance) and the 10-hop distance is 0.11, so 'tiny' is generous for 0.15. Wording concern for demo-builder; not covered by c9, which only covers the 'Heading down' and 'within 0.05' branches. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: The message 'Crawling: the hops are tiny.' fires for step sizes below 0.2 (factor above 0.6). At 0.15-0.19 the first hop is 1.2-1.5 of a 4.0 distance (30-38%), not tiny. Code behaviour is as stated; the displayed wording is not. Fix: 'Slow: each hop covers only a small share of the distance' or lower the threshold. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was 'Crawling: the hops are tiny.' (disputed: at 0.15-0.19 a hop is 30-38% of the distance). Each hop is 2*eta of the distance, under 40% when eta < 0.2, so the new message is exact. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Rechecked: message 'Slow: each hop covers under 40% of the distance left.' fires when factor 1-2*eta > 0.6, i.e. eta < 0.2, where a hop is 2*eta < 40% of the distance (node: eta 0.15 -> 30%, 0.19 -> 38%, 0.20 falls to the next branch).

recall.question: Gradient descent is zigzagging back and forth across a valley and getting no closer. What should you change?
options: Take more steps with the same size
recall.why: Zigzagging means each step overshoots the bottom. A smaller step size stops the overshoot; a bigger one makes it worse.
